item.content:encoded:
Stolen merchandise passes through two layers of hands: boosters are recruited to steal in stores, fences strip identifiers and resell, and the goods then go up on secondhand platforms. Connected goods fetch 70-80% of retail; T-shirts and deodorant only 30-something percent.

High information density: Home Depot's head of asset protection breaks down how shrink is categorized, the real P&L of locking up shelves, the pricing patterns of stolen goods, and the progress of federal legislation — lots of hard numbers.

8:19 A third of shrink is self-inflicted
Home Depot splits shrink into two buckets: operational/administrative and malicious — in Scott's phrasing, the things we do to ourselves and the things others do to us. At Home Depot, about 30% of shrink falls into the former, with the rest on the malicious side. The industry line that has circulated for years: of malicious shrink, about 40% is caused by internal employees, 35% by people who walk into the store, and the remainder is self-inflicted operational shrink. These percentages move only within a few points each year, but he thinks they are drifting upward, and that it has been underreported ever since COVID — neither police reports nor the FBI's Uniform Crime Report fully capture it.

22:52 Employees are explicitly told not to chase anyone
The bigger problem isn't money, it's people. Scott says professional criminals often use homeless people and addicts to go into stores and steal; these people have one thing on their minds — getting the goods out to trade for money — so they will get physical, and they have. People have been injured in Home Depot stores, and even killed. That's why asset protection staff are trained in de-escalation, and the 400,000 store employees are explicitly told not to intervene — just back off. His attitude: he'll trade shrink for human safety every day, and management and the board will back that decision.

23:53 RFID dies the moment it enters a steel store
Joe asks why RFID has been talked about for 25 years and in 2026 is still expensive and hard to scale. Scott says he doesn't understand it either, but explains Home Depot's particular situation: it's a hardware store, the store is full of steel, effectively a Faraday cage, so passive RFID can't be read — you have to use an active-signal approach. He also says tag cost is now almost zero; the real bottleneck is the reading hardware — covering a 140,000-square-foot sales floor with eight separate entrances and exits is extremely expensive. They've tried the idea of bricking merchandise before it leaves the store, but to do that for a single drill you'd have to rework the entire production line, and it's very hard to scale.

25:58 Stolen goods have been pushed onto secondhand platforms
The division of labor works like this: boosters are recruited and given a list, cash, or the promise of drugs to go steal from stores; the goods go to a fence — maybe a garage, a warehouse or a flea market — who strips price tags, store markings and electronic tags before reselling, and the money goes up to whoever runs the operation, which might be a small crew of a few people or a transnational gang. After the INFORM Act took effect in 2023, big platforms like Amazon and eBay were required to verify seller identities, so stolen goods shifted to Craigslist and Facebook Marketplace, because the law left a gap that doesn't cover peer-to-peer sellers. Home Depot works backward from the platforms, using models to flag sellers pricing below cost while moving large volumes.

35:19 One combo kit sold means 4.2 restocks
Whether to lock up shelves is a financial question. Scott says they look at the data: there's a $799 combo kit that has to be restocked 4.2 times for every one sold. Take that to finance and they immediately get it's a gross margin problem — as long as it breaks even or even makes a little, locking it up is justified. But half of Home Depot's revenue comes from professional contractors, and if they break a bit on the job site, rush to the store and find it out of stock, that's a loss too. So they lock up a carefully selected set of categories, with a QR code to summon an associate who unlocks in an average of 90 seconds; and locking up doesn't necessarily hurt sales — in some categories sales actually rise, because the product is finally there.

39:23 A fake bill of lading can just drive the goods away
In the supply chain he counts three plays: first, pure diversion, where a whole container is rerouted at the port or a transshipment warehouse and hauled somewhere else, even loaded back onto a container ship and sailed away; second, a driver drives eight hours across state lines, and while he sleeps someone pries open the trailer doors and unloads boxes; third, forged bills of lading and pickup orders, made to look real with AI, where a driver pulls in, says he's picking up a certain trailer, and just drives off. He says what's new isn't necessarily the methods, it's the volume, because these cases are very hard to pursue. Rail is the piece that has clearly worsened over the past five or six years — cars sitting in a yard get pried open by a group; and the other side has good intelligence, they don't touch every car, only the ones carrying guns or electronics.

41:28 AI in security is an efficiency tool
Scott says they have more cases than they can investigate, so for them AI is an efficiency question: a typical organized retail crime case takes an average of 70 days from discovery to closing and handing over to police, and compressing that cycle means they can work more cases. They just replaced the video management system across all 2,300 stores so existing cameras can run edge analytics — identifying people who linger too long in an area, deliberately avoid associates, or show up where they shouldn't be. He also admits that to identify a particular combination of suspicious behaviors and then recognize the specific person, he doesn't have enough cameras yet, but they will get there. Separately, they have an in-house company doing web scraping.

44:30 Seven years ago nobody cared; now there's a federal bill
He says he's very optimistic now. INFORM is arguably the first federal bill driven by organized retail crime, and next is CORCA (Combating Organized Retail Crime Act): the retail industry broadly supports it, it has bipartisan cosponsors, it has passed the House, it's attached to the NDAA awaiting Senate passage, and the president has said he'll sign it. The rationale is that this crime is inherently interstate — it happens in Cobb County, Georgia, and the goods flow to South Carolina and North Carolina, which is interstate transportation of stolen property, but there were no corresponding federal resources; the bill would provide resources, prosecutors and a coordination center. Seven years ago he was thoroughly pessimistic about this: nobody took it seriously, and the prevailing mood then was decriminalization and defunding the police.

item.title: Making Your Rivals Depend on Your System Is How America Has Won for Three Centuries
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-ilt-让对手依赖你的体系-是美国赢了三百年的秘密/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-ilt-让对手依赖你的体系-是美国赢了三百年的秘密/
item.description: The Dutch, the British and the Americans took turns as hegemon not by blockading rivals but by getting them to stake their survival on someone else's maritime order — once they can't live without the sea lanes and the markets, cutting them off becomes the most effective weapon short of war.
item.content:encoded:
The Dutch, the British and the Americans took turns as hegemon not by blockading rivals but by getting them to stake their survival on someone else's maritime order — once they can't live without the sea lanes and the markets, cutting them off becomes the most effective weapon short of war.

Walter Mead breaks America's three-century winning streak into a five-step strategy and pushes it all the way to China, the Taiwan Strait and AI deterrence. What you get is a durable judgment framework, not news-cycle opinion.

4:47 Unpredictability is a form of power
‘Unpredictability’ is not madness; it is a modern strategy of power. Mead says post-Cold War American diplomacy held itself up as a pillar of stability by ‘letting the whole world know where America's red lines are’, while Trump profits by doing the opposite: crossing lines, threatening allies, turning commitments into bargaining chips. He saw through a secret of the information age — the marginal cost of lying: the first lie is expensive, the thousandth is nearly free. When Clinton was engulfed by the Lewinsky scandal, he discovered that shame only lives in other people's minds; as long as you keep walking, the dogs bark and the caravan moves on. Trump took that insight to industrial scale. The cost is borne by the American diplomatic system: when the world's number one power turns itself into the unpredictable card, every alliance and rule built on predictability after World War II is coming apart faster.

10:00 The last step of global hegemony is cutting the cord
The Anglo-American maritime order did not win through any single battle but through a five-step playbook: first, an open society on an island — the 17th-century Dutch tolerated heretics and Jews, and ideas and capital poured in; then global trade, with Dutch merchant ships sailing the world, so wealthy that their paintings are full of Turkish carpets and Brazilian parrots; third, while continental powers fought over inland Silesia, you seized India and Canada across the globe. The fourth step is the riskiest: instead of copying Spain and sealing off your colonies, you invite the whole world in to do business, the British navy suppresses pirates, and every merchant ship benefits; Germany and Japan were likewise invited in after the war. Only the last step is the hole card: once the other side cannot live without your grain, your rubber and your shipping lanes, you cut it off — Germany discovered in World War I that Argentine grain and Malayan rubber had all been cut off, and its economy promptly collapsed.

16:38 Everything China does is to avoid having the cord cut
Look at China through the same framework and you find Beijing is well aware of its own vulnerability. Mead says: suppose the mainland blockades Taiwan, and the US counter-blockades from a hundred miles off Taiwan's coast: oil cannot get in, manufactured goods cannot get out, soybean contracts with Brazil and Argentina are voided, and China's economy is strangled alive. He has discussed these things with officials and scholars at Chinese universities, and this worry is always present. So China's energy policy has to be read side by side: on one hand building oil reserves so large they surprise outsiders; on the other, throwing up solar and hydropower while digging as much coal as possible. It is not schizophrenia, it is the same thing: pulling out, one by one, the soft spots of ‘dependence on the outside world’. He also warns the US not to retreat into isolationism — agriculture and AI both need overseas markets to feed themselves.

25:50 Every round of technology dividends needs new institutions to match
Mead starts from the ownership society: at America's founding there were independent farmers with land everywhere, and while a bridge is nice it raises my taxes — that trade-off is itself a political education. The railroad era came with the Homestead Act, the government giving land to railroad companies and farmers, and a national market grew out of it; in the 20th century what replaced the family farm was the single-family suburban house, paired with tax-exempt municipal bonds and highways, becoming a new wealth-distribution machine. Now that machine has hit housing prices: young people cannot afford to live near where they work. His remedy is remote work and autonomous driving. When the commuting radius expands from 40 miles to 75 miles, usable land for housing rises with the square of the radius, and the physical space opened by technology is enough to carry two more generations. But the precondition is filling in the institutional ‘infrastructure’ — he coined the word info-structure, meaning the institutions and regulatory rules that let AI actually land in hospitals and courts.

40:22 Silicon Valley is going over to the Tech Hamiltonian camp
American foreign policy debate has for centuries been four vocabularies: Hamiltonians want a strong state clearing the way for capital, Wilsonians want to spread liberal democracy, Jeffersonians fear a bigger government, Jacksonians stay isolationist in peacetime and hit as hard as they can when struck. The post-Cold War establishment was a marriage of Hamilton and Wilson, but Trump brought Jefferson and Jackson into the game. Mead says the new species truly worth watching is the Tech Hamiltonian. In the 1990s tech companies loved to say ‘we are a global company, Google has no borders, Washington has no say’; AI competition has turned tech into a contest of national destiny. Economic positions changed too: the old multinational car companies wanted borderless labor and markets, while Silicon Valley wants supply-chain and IP security, and even wants its employees to be patriotic, to feel that selling code to China is shameful, that a colleague will report you outright. The core of business has shifted from the old multinationals to tech nationalists, and this is the underwater current of America's political realignment.

50:00 The power with the most equipment fears technological turnover the most
Mead has been to Ukraine twice. The first time, at a drone factory, he saw them converting children's toy trucks into ground drones carrying mines to blow up tanks; a few months later, the progress was unimaginably fast. The battlefield is now a gray kill zone, usually only two or three soldiers moving together, and one of the hardest problems is ‘how to get the wounded out’ — you need a ground drone with a metal shield to drag a person, with a squad of drones alongside hunting the enemy's drones coming to attack. He heard of one wounded soldier who took 63 days to be evacuated from the front. The changes flip every six months. The bitterest irony for the US: the power with the most tanks and aircraft carriers is precisely the one most afraid of this kind of parameter revolution — existing equipment turns from an advantage into a relocation cost. Russia's Black Sea Fleet has no great battle to fight, yet it is bottled up at home by Ukraine's small boats and drones.

54:16 The new variable most worth watching in the Taiwan Strait is Japan
On whether the mainland will attack Taiwan, Mead's judgment is that Beijing needs a very high probability of success before it will cross the threshold — failure would be catastrophic for the initiator. But between ‘attack’ and ‘do nothing’ there is a long gray ladder: for example, requiring all merchant ships bound for Taiwan to first stop at mainland ports for customs clearance, or imposing a soft blockade, doing things that change facts enough without triggering an armed US response. The real new variable on the Taiwan board is not America's attitude but Japan. The Japanese have already publicly concluded that if China takes Taiwan, Japanese independence is finished too; they are raising defense budgets, rewriting security doctrine, reshaping the national psyche. Historically Japan pivots fast when facing a real threat. How steep Japan's learning curve is, and whether Beijing's calculations must factor Japan in, is the key to the Taiwan question in the coming years.

1:10:00 AI actually makes deterrence more credible
Moving Cold War deterrence logic into the algorithmic age, Mead points to a counterintuitive corollary: deterrence succeeds or fails on making the opponent one hundred percent believe that ‘if I do X, you will necessarily do Y, and you can do it and are willing to’. As long as there is a human veto point in the decision chain that says ‘I might soften when the time comes’, that commitment has a crack. Automating part of foreign-policy decision-making and handing it to AI turns retaliation into an executable mechanism that will not hesitate — deterrence becomes more credible. But this is the doomsday machine problem from science fiction: decisions of civilizational scale no longer require a human to bear the consequences. His own assessment of the question is that it is ‘very interesting and also a bit confusing’, and he does not think the answer has appeared yet.

item.title: ECT Is Not What You Think: A Century of Drift from Back Room to Routine Treatment
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-tpwky-ect-不是你想的那样-从密室到常规治疗的百年漂移/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-tpwky-ect-不是你想的那样-从密室到常规治疗的百年漂移/
item.description: Modern ECT is a procedure performed under anesthesia and muscle relaxants, with strong efficacy, but the evidence on memory-loss side effects is still incomplete, and social misunderstanding has left it over-stigmatized.
item.content:encoded:
Modern ECT is a procedure performed under anesthesia and muscle relaxants, with strong efficacy, but the evidence on memory-loss side effects is still incomplete, and social misunderstanding has left it over-stigmatized.

If your image of ECT is still stuck on One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, this episode will overhaul it. Hear the actual procedure, the indications, the side effects, and one expert's clinical account.

8:07 What actually happens if you or I get ECT
If you or I were to receive ECT, the steps go like this: first a risk assessment and informed consent, then a physical exam, then an overnight fast. The next morning, in a hospital or outpatient setting, an IV line goes in along with two blood pressure cuffs (arm and right leg), and EKG, EEG and EMG leads are attached. After the anesthesiologist puts you to sleep, the leg cuff is inflated to restrict blood flow to the right foot, then a muscle relaxant such as succinylcholine is given. Once the muscles are fully relaxed, a bite block is placed, and a brief pulse of current is delivered through the electrodes (lasting seconds, or even half a second). The goal is not to make your whole body convulse, but to induce a generalized seizure, typically lasting 25-70 seconds. Because the muscles are relaxed, you see almost no external movement — the whole thing is obvious on the EEG.

14:15 Electrode placement, and why the right side comes first
There are several electrode placements: bitemporal (the way it looks in the movies), bifrontal, and most commonly 'right unilateral' — one electrode on the right temple, the other on the right side of the top of the head. Right unilateral is used for most people because it produces fewer cognitive side effects. Why consider the right side first? Because for about 98% of right-handed people and 70%-90% of left-handed people, language function sits in the left temporal lobe. Avoiding electrical stimulation on the left side theoretically reduces language-related memory problems. But right unilateral is slightly less effective than bilateral. During a course of treatment, doctors switch based on side effects and efficacy: if bilateral side effects are heavy, switch to right unilateral; if right unilateral isn't working well enough, switch to bilateral.

16:20 Seizure threshold and the effective dose
The seizure threshold is the minimum amount of current that can induce a seizure. There is no precise measuring device, so you start by estimating from age, then probe upward from a low dose until a seizure appears. But treatment isn't just about reaching threshold — the effective dose is usually 2.5 to 5 times the threshold. With bilateral, 2.5 times is enough, whereas right unilateral needs 5 times, because unilateral stimulation has a harder time achieving the same effect. The dose varies from person to person and has to be adjusted as you go. If in one session a patient's seizure doesn't occur or doesn't last long enough (under 25 seconds), the doctor may increase the dose and try again. Treatment is generally three times a week, with a full course of 6 to 18 sessions, sometimes longer.

20:22 We still don't know exactly how ECT works
Why does shocking the brain treat depression and catatonia? Frankly: we still don't fully understand. There are several main hypotheses. One is neurotransmitter change: after ECT, serotonin, dopamine and GABA (an inhibitory transmitter) all shift markedly. The rise in GABA is itself anticonvulsant, which could explain why the seizure threshold rises and seizures get shorter over a course of treatment. Two, large hormonal fluctuations in ACTH, prolactin and TSH are seen in the hypothalamus and pituitary. Three, ECT promotes neurogenesis, with BDNF (brain-derived neurotrophic factor) as a key molecule. But how these changes directly relieve symptoms still has no one-to-one mechanism. The mechanism may also differ by condition (depression, schizophrenia, catatonia), so for now the only option is to keep researching.

24:24 Depression data: far better than first-line antidepressants
For treating severe depression, ECT's key numbers are quite strong: most studies report remission rates (symptoms fully gone) of 50%-60%, and response rates (marked improvement) of 60%-90%. By comparison, the best remission rate for SSRI antidepressants is only about 40%. ECT has another uncommon benefit — it can cut the 30-day readmission rate by half. This is not to say it should be first choice, nor that it has no risks (relapse or symptom rebound within 6-12 months is still not rare); but in patients with treatment-resistant depression plus severe suicide risk, these efficacy advantages are hard to ignore.

26:27 Memory problems draw the most attention among side effects
ECT's thorniest side effects center on cognition and memory. Right after the procedure there is brief confusion lasting from a few dozen seconds to half an hour, and for weeks there may be declines in attention and executive function. Interestingly, most cognitive function actually improves in the long term — possibly because the depression improves. The real trouble is memory. Anterograde amnesia (difficulty forming new memories) usually recovers within a few weeks after the course ends, which is why many people are restricted from driving or making major decisions during treatment. Retrograde amnesia (losing past memories) is what worries patients more: it typically affects recall of the most recent months or even years before treatment, and in most cases recovers, but in some it is permanent. Bilateral treatment is more likely to cause this than right unilateral.

34:55 Catatonia: a frequently misread, potentially fatal syndrome
Catatonia is often lumped in as a subtype of schizophrenia, but it is actually a psychomotor syndrome that any psychiatric or neurological illness can trigger. Patients appear awake, eyes open, yet are almost completely motionless and mute; they may lie rigid or show waxy flexibility (an arm placed in a position stays there). Because they cannot eat or drink and remain immobile for long periods, malnutrition, pressure sores, muscle contractures and even death become likely. Untreated catatonia has a mortality rate as high as 20%! The most common treatment is benzodiazepines, but ECT is extremely effective in catatonia from many causes. The girl with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis mentioned earlier (the 'Brain on Fire' case) developed catatonia, and when both immunotherapy and lorazepam failed, she ultimately recovered with ECT.

48:36 The biggest bottleneck is not efficacy but access
Dr. Lopez believes the biggest obstacle ECT faces today is finding a place to get it. His hospital performs more than 6,000 treatments a year across two campuses, averaging about 10-12 per patient. But it is not widely available across the US, and adults and children traveling across state lines for care are not few — especially in infants, children and adolescents with catatonia from autoimmune encephalitis, where finding an experienced treatment team is extremely hard. So improving access is his greatest hope. At the same time, doctors on other internal medicine, pediatric and critical care teams often don't recognize catatonia and don't dare, or don't think, to call an ECT consult; so 'preaching' to non-psychiatric colleagues is part of his daily work.

item.title: The Supreme Court Gave Students Constitutional Rights, Then Handed Searches and Paddlings Back to the Schools
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-stuffmissed-美国最高法院先给了学生宪法权利-后来又把搜包和体罚还给校园/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-stuffmissed-美国最高法院先给了学生宪法权利-后来又把搜包和体罚还给校园/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: From refusing to salute the flag to having a purse searched, six cases gradually drew the constitutional rights of American public school students; the Supreme Court laid down that schools are not totalitarian enclaves while also holding that corporal punishment and reasonable-suspicion searches do not violate the Constitution, and the boundary of those rights narrowed accordingly.
item.content:encoded:
From refusing to salute the flag to having a purse searched, six cases gradually drew the constitutional rights of American public school students; the Supreme Court laid down that schools are not totalitarian enclaves while also holding that corporal punishment and reasonable-suspicion searches do not violate the Constitution, and the boundary of those rights narrowed accordingly.

Each case gets five or six minutes laying out the background and the holding, suited to listeners who want to grasp in one sitting where the lines fall on speech, corporal punishment and searches in American public schools.

5:10 The flag-salute case: student rights enter the schoolhouse for the first time
Can students really invoke the First Amendment in class? This case actually begins with religion: Jehovah's Witnesses families held that saluting the flag violated the commandments against having other gods and against graven images, and refused to pledge or salute the flag. In 1940 the Supreme Court had ruled against them, and World War II pushed more school districts to require students to salute and recite the pledge daily. West Virginia expelled students who refused the pledge, labeled them delinquents, and their parents could be fined or even jailed. In 1943 the Supreme Court overturned the earlier ruling 6-3, and Justice Jackson wrote the opinion on Flag Day: orthodoxy in politics, nationalism, religion or other matters of opinion is not to be defined by any official; students need not utter words they do not believe, nor make empty gestures. This was the first time the Court established that students hold some First Amendment rights inside school.

11:21 An official prayer text is held unconstitutional
In the Cold War the United States cast itself as a God-fearing nation, added Under God to the Pledge of Allegiance in 1954, and more public schools began reading scripture or praying before class. In 1951 the New York State Board of Regents asked religious leaders to co-write a short, non-denominational prayer, with each district deciding whether to adopt it. Districts that used the prayer let students opt out, but the parents of 10 students still sued. In 1962 Engel v. Vitale held it unconstitutional 6-1; the key was not whether it was compulsory but that the prayer was written by the government, which itself constituted establishing religion. Justice Black quoted Madison: it is proper to take alarm at the first experiment on our liberties; the same authority that could establish Christianity to the exclusion of other religions could easily establish one Christian sect. The ruling provoked fierce backlash, and the plaintiff families were mocked and harassed.

18:31 An armband is constitutional expression
In December 1965, middle and high school students in Des Moines planned to wear black armbands to class to protest American involvement in the Vietnam War. School officials announced in advance that refusal to remove them would mean suspension, and some students — including four siblings — wore the armbands anyway and were suspended. In 1969 the Supreme Court ruled for the students 7-2. The issue was that this was not ordinary dress or grooming but quiet, passive expression close to pure speech, and it did not disrupt class. Absent evidence of actual or demonstrable substantial interference with teaching, school officials may not suppress student opinion. The ruling said public schools may not become totalitarian enclaves, and students and teachers do not shed their constitutional rights at the schoolhouse gate. This substantial disruption standard later became the baseline for free speech on campus. Justice Black dissented that students would from then on resist almost every school rule, and the host says on the show that this slippery-slope argument sounds rather absurd.

24:40 A school-funded newspaper can be censored
In 1983 two pieces in the Hazelwood East High School student newspaper The Spectrum troubled principal Reynolds: a story on teen pregnancy that used pseudonyms but might still allow the interviewees to be identified, and a divorce story that named and criticized a student's parent. Reynolds decided to cut both full pages rather than just remove the articles, on the grounds that he had no time to revise and the paper had to come out before the semester ended. In 1988 the Supreme Court ruled for the school 5-3. The key distinction was between tolerating student speech and promoting it: this newspaper was funded and published by the school, readers would take its contents as endorsed by the school, and the two pieces were indeed ethically immature as journalism. The Court held that school officials may exercise control over what they promote. The rights established in Tinker were thus given their first clear boundary.

29:46 Corporal punishment is not an Eighth Amendment matter
Host Tracy suddenly recalls that many of her childhood teachers kept wooden paddles on their desks, and on looking it up finds corporal punishment has still not died out in the United States. In the 1977 case Ingram v. Wright, the school's paddle was under two feet long, three or four inches wide and half an inch thick, with one to five swats in principle; but Ingram was struck more than 20 times in a single incident and needed medical attention. The Supreme Court did not dwell on whether that individual case was excessive, but held that school corporal punishment does not violate the Constitution. The reasoning was that the Eighth Amendment protects the convicted, and prisoners and schoolchildren are separated by the harsh facts of criminal conviction and imprisonment; schools are open places, with teachers and classmates as witnesses, and students go home at the end of the day. According to NEA figures, corporal punishment remains legal in public schools in 17 states and is actually practiced in 14, with boys, Black students and students with disabilities struck at significantly higher rates.

33:52 A bag search needs only reasonable suspicion
In 1980 in New Jersey, a 14-year-old student known as TLO was reported by a teacher for smoking in the restroom. Vice principal Choplik searched her purse, saw cigarettes and rolling papers, kept digging, and found what appeared to be marijuana and evidence of drug dealing; TLO was ultimately convicted and given a year's probation. In 1985 the Supreme Court upheld the search 6-3. The ruling acknowledged that the Fourth Amendment binds school officials and that students have a privacy expectation, but that it must be balanced against the school's need to maintain a learning environment. So school searches need not meet the probable cause police require, only the lower threshold of reasonable suspicion. The teacher's report that TLO was smoking gave the vice principal reason to suspect she had cigarettes, and a purse is exactly where they would be; seeing rolling papers naturally extended the suspicion to marijuana, which was equally reasonable.

item.title: To Make Criticism Land, Lead With High Standards and Trust
